title: The Disruption Machine: What the Gospel of Innovation Gets Wrong
author: Jill Lepore

dom.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s caution against treating technology adoption as inherently valuable, adding a broader methodological critique of disruption narratives and concrete examples in which attempted self-disruption caused severe organisational harm. It does not address legal AI’s task-level capabilities, verification or workflow design directly.
qs: It’s mostly recipes.”  Cartoon by Sam Gross  The handpicked case study, which is Christensen’s method, is a notoriously weak foundation on which to build a theory.

Morrison-Knudsen announced in 1995 that it had lost three hundred and fifty million dollars, by which point the company had essentially collapsed—not because it didn’t disruptively innovate but because it did.

st.t: Disruption theory: Historical examples weakly fit predictions
st.an: Lepore directly supports the cluster’s proposition by challenging the historical reliability, predictive performance and retrospective classification of disruption theory. Her counterexamples and institutional critique reinforce the synthesis’s conclusion that industry change does not validate Christensen’s specific causal mechanism or justify disruption as a universal prescription.
qs: The strength of a prediction made from a model depends on the quality of the historical evidence and on the reliability of the methods used to gather and interpret it.

mo.t: Business disruption: Incumbents must separate experiments credibly
Institutional reform: Outsider ideas need insider adoption

kp.k: Disruption theory explains incumbent failure through otherwise sound decisions
kp.d: Lepore reports Christensen’s argument that established companies can fail because they rationally prioritize existing customers and sustaining improvements, missing cheaper, initially inferior products serving less profitable customers that eventually take over an industry. This is the theory she critiques, not her own endorsed account. The article concerns business history and institutional change rather than AI or legal services directly.
qs: doing the right thing is the wrong thing
the selling of a cheaper, poorer-quality product

kp.k: Disruption rhetoric converts uncertainty into pressure for radical change
kp.d: Lepore interprets disruption’s popularity as a historically situated response to financial and global anxiety. She argues that consultants, investors and institutional leaders promote urgency while treating criticism of disruption theory as opposition to change itself. Her account distinguishes novelty from improvement and challenges the assumption that innovation necessarily advances human welfare.
qs: Replacing “progress” with “innovation” skirts the question of whether a novelty is an improvement
a language of panic, fear, asymmetry, and disorder

kp.k: Historical models require stronger evidence than selected success stories
kp.d: Lepore argues that a theory claiming both to explain past events and predict future ones depends on reliable historical evidence and methods. She criticizes Christensen’s handpicked case studies, definitions of success, sources and treatment of counterevidence, asserting that the historical conditions of proof have not been met.
qs: The handpicked case study, which is Christensen’s method, is a notoriously weak foundation
None of these conditions have been met.

kp.k: Disk-drive outcomes depend on classification and observation windows
kp.d: Christensen classified 111 of 116 disk-drive technologies as sustaining and five as disruptive. Lepore questions his shifting classifications of entrants and incumbents and his original success criterion: more than fifty million dollars in revenues in constant 1987 dollars in any single year between 1977 and 1989, even for firms subsequently withdrawing. She contrasts his treatment of Seagate with its sales doubling between 1989 and 1990 to $2.4 billion and its industry-leading nine billion dollars in revenues in 1997.
qs: Much of the theory of disruptive innovation rests on this arbitrary definition of success.
In fact, Seagate Technology was not felled by disruption.

kp.k: Long-term disk-drive survival highlights continuity and incremental improvement
kp.d: Lepore reports that, after consolidation, divisions dominating the disk-drive industry in 2014 were divisions already leading in the nineteen-eighties, sometimes under different ownership. She contrasts this continuity with the subsequent failure of celebrated entrants, including Micropolis and MiniScribe; MiniScribe was investigated for fraud in 1989 and soon collapsed. Her qualified conclusion is that incremental improvement appears more important to long-term success than being first with a new format.
qs: more striking, from the vantage of history, are the continuities
Companies that were quick to release a new product but not skilled at tinkering

kp.k: Excavator history challenges entrant classifications and incumbent failure narratives
kp.d: Christensen counted thirty established excavator companies in the nineteen-fifties, with only four surviving by the nineteen-seventies against thirteen disruptive newcomers. Lepore counters that several supposed newcomers already made cable-operated shovels. She reports that Bucyrus’s sales grew sevenfold and profits twenty-five-fold between 1962 and 1979, identifies industry-wide macroeconomic pressures and a disastrous leveraged buyout in its later difficulties, and notes Caterpillar’s purchase of the company for nearly nine billion dollars in 2011.
qs: many of Christensen’s “new entrants” had been making cable-operated shovels for years
between 1962 and 1979 Bucyrus’s sales grew sevenfold and its profits grew twenty-five-fold

kp.k: Selective sourcing and dismissed counterevidence weaken organizational prescriptions
kp.d: Lepore criticizes reliance on a founders’ foundation account as the single source for the motor-controls case. She also challenges the retail evidence for Christensen’s claim that competing business models require separate organizations: Kmart and Target were treated as successes and in-house Woolco as a failure, while Kmart’s closures were omitted from the main account and its troubles dismissed as unrelated. She notes Kmart’s 2002 bankruptcy.
qs: Christensen’s sources are often dubious and his logic questionable.
two models for how to make money cannot peacefully coexist within a single organization

kp.k: Steel disruption accounts omit potentially relevant labor arrangements
kp.d: Christensen reported U.S. Steel cutting production requirements from nine labor-hours per ton in 1980 to just under three in 1991, alongside workforce reductions from more than 93,000 to fewer than 23,000. Lepore argues that his explanation omits a 1986–1987 labor action involving twenty-two thousand workers and differences between unionized incumbents and generally non-union minimills. She acknowledges U.S. Steel’s grave difficulties but disputes treating its failure as established historical fact.
qs: Christensen tends to ignore factors that don’t support his theory.
its failure is by no means a matter of historical record

kp.k: Prominent failed forecasts challenge disruption theory’s predictive authority
kp.d: Lepore reports that Christensen’s $3.8-million Disruptive Growth Fund, launched March 10, 2000, was liquidated less than a year later after losing sixty-four per cent while the Nasdaq lost fifty per cent. She contrasts his 2007 prediction that Apple would not succeed with the iPhone against its first five years generating a hundred and fifty billion dollars of revenue. These examples support her criticism that apparent predictive success often depends on retrospective labeling.
qs: the prediction of the theory would be that Apple won’t succeed with the iPhone
Disruptive innovation can reliably be seen only after the fact.

kp.k: Circular explanations insulate disruption from contrary outcomes
kp.d: Lepore argues that advocates can interpret every outcome as confirmation: incumbent failure proves insufficient disruption, startup failure exemplifies disruptive experimentation, and incumbent success merely postpones failure. She distinguishes this circular reasoning from the evolutionary theory to which Christensen compares disruption.
qs: the advocates of disruption have an affinity for circular arguments
When an established company succeeds, that’s only because it hasn’t yet failed.

kp.k: Pursuing disruption can destroy rather than preserve businesses
kp.d: Explicitly working within the case-study approach she criticizes, Lepore offers counterexamples to prescriptions for self-disruption. Morrison-Knudsen’s move into train-car businesses preceded a reported three hundred and fifty million dollar loss and effective collapse in 1995. Time, Inc.’s Pathfinder website, launched in 1994 at an estimated cost exceeding a hundred million dollars, was abandoned in 1999. She argues that unsuccessful experiments can disappear from retrospective accounts while successes become evidence for disruption.
qs: not because it didn’t disruptively innovate but because it did
Had Pathfinder been successful, it would have been greeted, retrospectively, as evidence of disruptive innovation.

kp.k: Financial innovation illustrates systemic harm and successful restraint
kp.d: Lepore characterizes subprime mortgages, collateralized debt obligations and mortgage-backed securities as disruptive innovations that contributed to the global financial crisis. She contrasts these with TD Bank CEO Ed Clark’s rejection of asset-backed commercial paper and expansion of traditional banking services. She reports TD Bank’s assets increasing from $278 billion to $806 billion between 2002 and 2012 and argues that crises generated by disruption can intensify the anxiety sustaining its appeal.
qs: When the financial-services industry disruptively innovated, it led to a global financial crisis.
the meltdown didn’t dim the fervor for disruption; instead, it fuelled it

kp.k: Public-serving institutions have obligations beyond commercial performance
kp.d: Lepore argues that business-origin theories have been extended to schools, universities, hospitals, museums, churches and journalism despite their different purposes. Although these institutions have revenues, expenses and sometimes profits, she maintains that obligations to patients, students, congregations, readers and the public cannot be reduced to earnings or commodity production. This is her central qualification on transferring industrial disruption models across domains.
qs: People aren’t disk drives.
obligations that lie outside the realm of earnings

kp.k: University disruption prescriptions rest on disputed historical analogies
kp.d: Lepore reports that Christensen and Henry J. Eyring recommended blended online and face-to-face learning and that their 2011 book contributed to enthusiasm for MOOCs. She links disruption rhetoric to the University of Virginia trustees’ attempted removal of its president in 2012. She criticizes their assessment of seventeenth-century Harvard through contemporary instructional criteria, contrasting thirteen students in 1640 with twenty-one thousand in 2014, while explicitly allowing that online education may have other valid justifications.
qs: That doesn’t mean good arguments can’t be made for online education.
there’s nothing factually persuasive in this account of its historical urgency and even inevitability

kp.k: Innovation prescriptions conflict over organizational separation
kp.d: Lepore reports Christensen’s recommendation for autonomous innovation teams insulated from existing customer demands and immediate profit pressures. She contrasts this with the New York Times Innovation Report’s proposal to abandon the newsroom–business wall as an obstacle to innovation. She argues that the wall historically protected the public interest, not merely office efficiency, whereas the report proposed a shared focus on Reader Experience measured in Attention Minutes.
qs: The “heavyweight innovation team”? That’s what journalists used to call the “newsroom.”
the important business interests of institutions like the press might at times conflict

kp.k: Disruption is a limited theory, not inevitable historical destiny
kp.d: Lepore concludes that disruptive innovation is a historically situated theory of business failure rather than a general explanation of change or a law of nature. She criticizes investor rhetoric encouraging recklessness, remorselessness and quick exits, and emphasizes continuity and uncertainty rather than confidently prescribing or forecasting a universal disruptive future.
qs: It’s not a law of nature.
Transfixed by change, it’s blind to continuity.
It makes a very poor prophet.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lepore argues that disruptive innovation is an unreliable predictor of business change, rather than an inevitable law of incumbent displacement.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about innovation, business history and public-serving institutions; it makes no claims about AI or legal services. Lepore argues that disruption theory relies on selectively interpreted historical cases, overlooks continuity and incremental improvement, and can accommodate contradictory outcomes retrospectively. In disk drives, she argues that longer-term success appears to favor manufacturers skilled at incremental improvement, not necessarily those first to introduce new formats. These are Lepore's claims, distinct from the pro-disruption prescriptions she quotes from Christensen and other advocates.

pts.k: Lepore argues that adopting disruptive strategies can damage businesses, while maintaining and improving established services can support success.
pts.d: She presents Morrison-Knudsen's diversification into train manufacturing and Time Inc.'s Pathfinder venture as counterexamples to the prescription that established businesses must disrupt themselves. She contrasts financial-sector innovations associated with the global financial crisis with TD Bank's rejection of asset-backed commercial paper and expansion of traditional banking. Her argument challenges the necessity and benefits of disruption; it does not establish a universal prediction that innovation fails or incumbents survive.

pts.k: Lepore argues that exporting disruption prescriptions to education, healthcare and journalism disregards obligations beyond earnings.
pts.d: She links disruption advocacy to universities' rush toward online education and to pressure to remove the separation between editorial and commercial work in journalism. She argues that the historical case for online education's urgency or inevitability is unpersuasive, while explicitly allowing that online education may have sound arguments in its favor. Her journalism discussion presents public-interest obligations as potentially conflicting with business interests, rather than treating audience-attention measures as sufficient institutional goals.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Lepore supports her predictive critique with historical counterexamples, financial figures and two unsuccessful applications of disruption theory.
pts.d: She reports that Seagate's sales doubled between 1989 and 1990 to $2.4 billion and that it remained the largest disk-drive company in 1997 with $9 billion in revenues. She contrasts this with the failure of celebrated entrants, including Micropolis and MiniScribe. She disputes the classification of established excavator manufacturers as entrants and reports that Bucyrus's sales increased sevenfold and profits twenty-five-fold between 1962 and 1979. She also cites a disruption-based investment fund's 64% loss against a 50% Nasdaq decline, and contrasts Christensen's 2007 prediction of iPhone failure with $150 billion in revenue during its first five years. These are historical and financial counterexamples, not a systematic predictive validation study.

pts.k: The business-risk and institutional claims rest on selected cases, documentary analysis and normative argument.
pts.d: Lepore reports Morrison-Knudsen's $350 million loss in 1995, Pathfinder's estimated cost exceeding $100 million before abandonment in 1999, and TD Bank's asset growth from $278 billion in 2002 to $806 billion in 2012. For education, she examines Christensen and Eyring's historical account of Harvard and connects their 2011 book to enthusiasm for MOOCs and the University of Virginia trustees' attempted removal of its president. For journalism, she analyzes the New York Times' 2014 Innovation Report and its proposed changes to editorial-business separation. Her claims about distinctive professional obligations are historical and normative arguments, not measured effects on educational, clinical or journalistic outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The critique is anchored in evidence available by June 2014 and emphasizes that conclusions change with the observation window.
pts.d: Lpore's cases span nineteenth-century institutional origins through 2014, with much of the business evidence concentrated in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. She challenges Christensen's original 1977–1989 success window, which counted firms exceeding a revenue threshold in any single year even if they later withdrew. Following firms beyond that cutoff reveals incumbent survival and entrant failures. She offers no dated forecast of future market change. Her qualifications include that disruption theory concerns business failure rather than all change, that first-mover success need not persist, and that criticism of disruption theory is not opposition to change or online education.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are incumbent businesses, entrants, investors, workers and institutions serving obligations beyond commerce.
pts.d: For established businesses and investors, Lepore's argument concerns potentially costly strategies premised on inevitable displacement. For startups and their workers, she describes high failure rates, short employment tenures and pressure toward recklessness. For universities, disruption rhetoric influences governance and instructional strategy; students and teachers are affected. For journalism, proposed removal of editorial-commercial boundaries affects journalists, readers and the public interest. She also identifies patients, congregations and museum audiences as beneficiaries of institutional obligations that cannot be reduced to earnings. No legal-market segment or AI-specific role is discussed.
